sources.entry: The Next 700 Stateless Services, Henning Rohde. This article is part of a series of four articles that challenge the stateless microservice approach. A very refreshing take, very well written.

summary.title: The Next 700 Stateless Services
summary.one_liner: Stateless services are not as simple or scalable as they look: the strict design trades latency for simplicity, and its costs show up in scope, database scale, background work and the wider system.
takeaways: A standard stateless service is request-driven, has no node-to-node communication, and is split into frontend, business and database layers.
The strict flavor runs each request as one transaction, which makes it simple and scalable but adds latency from database round trips.
Splitting work into strict stateless services can create atomicity and correctness problems across services, so the whole system must be judged, not each service alone.
Scale, background processing and latency each add complexity; caching is tempting but can turn loose services into incorrect ones.
summary.summary: The article argues that statelessness has become a near-universal label that says little, since most services still manage state through an external database or broker. It describes the standard three-layer stateless service and two variants, strict (one transaction per request, like CRUD wrappers) and loose (multiple transactions or non-transactional state such as caches). It then examines the tradeoffs of the strict design: latency, scope that pushes toward microservices, database scaling demands, and the lack of support for background work. A worked example, a fictional pizza ordering system split across three services, shows how cross-service atomicity problems emerge even when each service looks clean. The author is critical of uncritical overuse of this design, and suggests weighing the actual tradeoffs instead.
